method.title: A cycle of six steps.
method.lead: What I learn when I deliver comes back in as a problem.
method.ring: The method's cycle: pick a step

steps.name: Understand the problem
steps.text: Before building, I understand the context and the business. Talking to the people who use the software changes what gets prioritised.
steps.example: In-person day with clients in Buenos Aires (April 2026): demos, alignment and direct conversation about their real challenges.

steps.name: Align and negotiate priorities
steps.text: I agree on scope and priorities before writing code, and I hold the difficult conversations when they are needed.
steps.example: At Tsoft I take part in technical decisions with the team and support people who join.

steps.name: Design
steps.text: I design the interface and the system together: rules, states and limits before pretty screens.
steps.example: Volta and DentalOS: navigable demos with their own identity and labelled data.

steps.name: Build in stages
steps.text: I split the work into small batches, each with its acceptance criteria.
steps.example: Eclipse moves forward in documented batches, with approval gates.

steps.name: Show and validate
steps.text: I show something that works as early as possible and test it: automated tests, visual QA and demos.
steps.example: Velmar: a navigable demo for a client, with sample data.

steps.name: Deliver and learn
steps.text: I ship with CI/CD, document what I learned and apply it again.
steps.example: At Tsoft I work with deployment pipelines, integrations and CI/CD on Telefónica and Tuenti projects.

system.title: An agentic system, split into parts.
system.lead: I program with agents: each one has its part, and a person approves every delivery.
system.skills: Loads its skills depending on the task.

ask.label: Request
ask.note: Everything starts with something someone needs to solve.

chief.label: Direction
chief.note: Decides what gets done and in what order; the code is for the role agents.

spec.label: Spec
spec.note: A short document: problem, scope, acceptance criteria and how to roll back.

roles.label: Role agents
roles.note: Each agent takes its part of the batch and loads the skills the task asks for.

qa.label: Tests and QA
qa.note: Every claim carries its level of evidence; what fails goes back to the agents.

gate.label: Human gate
gate.note: I authorise publishing, spending and changing prices.

ship.label: Publish
ship.note: It is published once I give my OK, and what was learned goes back into the method.

chief.name: Direction
chief.role: Owns the plan, the scope and the cost: decides what gets done and in what order.

uxui.name: UX/UI
uxui.role: Flows, states and accessibility before screens.

design.name: Design
design.role: Visual system, type, colour and motion, with a review rubric.

ads.name: Ads
ads.role: Pieces and hooks for campaigns, with honesty rules.

frontend.name: Frontend architect
frontend.role: Project analysis, components, data integration and performance.

backend.name: Backend architect
backend.role: Layers, schemas, services and transactions, always discovery first.

security.name: Cybersecurity
security.role: Threat modelling, OWASP and hardening; tests only in our own environments.

game.name: Game architect
game.role: Mechanics, reward economies and web game performance.

trailer.name: Trailer architect
trailer.role: Direction, storyboard, motion and sound for pieces like my trailer.

levels.d: A document or a source says so.
It ran on my machine, with its tests.
It runs where it is used.

items.d: Eleven agents with separate responsibilities, with skills that load depending on the task.
Every change starts with a short document: problem, scope, acceptance criteria and how to roll back.
I tell apart what I read, what I tested locally and what runs in a real environment, and I label it.
I authorise publishing, spending and changing prices.
Automated tests, end-to-end journeys with Playwright and CI that runs the tests and the build.
Every redesign is compared with the previous one at several widths and with reduced motion, in Chromium.
Everything fictional says «Demo», and every new dependency or expense goes through my OK.
